Between January 2023 and December 2025, investigators systematically evaluated acute respiratory tract infections in children under eighteen years of age, identifying human metapneumovirus in nearly twelve percent of systematically screened hospital admissions. The research uncovered a notable temporal transition in the age distribution of affected children, marked by a progressive shift from older children toward younger infants over the consecutive surveillance years. The study also characterized co-circulating viral lineages, identified distinct amino acid substitutions within the viral fusion protein in emerging strains, and detailed clinical outcomes across varying levels of hospital care, providing comprehensive epidemiological evidence on pediatric human metapneumovirus activity during the post-pandemic recovery era. Human metapneumovirus was initially identified in 2001 as a widespread respiratory pathogen belonging to the Pneumoviridae family, sharing genetic relationships with respiratory syncytial virus. Worldwide pooled prevalence estimates indicate that the virus accounts for approximately 5.3 percent of respiratory tract infections across all age brackets, reaching its highest documented prevalence of 6.7 percent among children younger than five years and falling to 2.5 percent among adults. The viral genome spans roughly 13,300 base pairs encoding eight genes, with the fusion protein serving as the primary neutralizing antibody target and both the fusion and attachment glycoprotein genes utilized for molecular classification. The pathogen divides into two major genotypes, designated A and B, comprising four circulating sublineages termed A1, A2, B1, and B2. Following extensive disruptions to typical viral seasonality during the COVID-19 pandemic, widespread post-pandemic resurgences were recorded internationally, yet comprehensive clinical and molecular data within Taiwanese healthcare settings remained sparse. To evaluate these dynamics, researchers implemented a hybrid retrospective and prospective cohort protocol collaborating between the National Taiwan University Children’s Hospital, an academic tertiary medical center situated in northern Taiwan, and the Show Chwan Healthcare System, encompassing two community hospitals located in Changhua County within central Taiwan. The investigation enrolled hospitalized children younger than eighteen years diagnosed with acute respiratory illness who underwent molecular testing with either the BioFire FilmArray Respiratory Panel 2.1 or the Pneumonia Panel. Period 1 spanned January 2023 through June 2024 as a retrospective electronic medical record review, while Period 2 operated prospectively from July 2024 through December 2025, gathering nasopharyngeal swabs and structured clinical records after obtaining written informed parental consent. Across the entire cohort, lower respiratory tract illness was classified by attending physicians into bronchitis, bronchiolitis, bronchopneumonia, or pneumonia, while dyspnea was documented by observable nasal flaring or intercostal and subcostal retractions. Across the thirty-six months of hospital surveillance, clinical teams performed molecular screening panels on 3310 hospitalized pediatric admissions presenting with acute respiratory conditions, identifying at least one causative respiratory pathogen in 2652 individuals, representing 80.1 percent of all screened tests. Rhinovirus or enterovirus appeared as the most prevalent detected agent at 38.2 percent, followed in frequency by respiratory syncytial virus at 15.2 percent, parainfluenza viruses at 14.8 percent, adenovirus at 14.4 percent, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae at 12.3 percent. Human metapneumovirus ranked as the sixth most frequent pathogen, detected in 390 patients, or 11.8 percent of tested cases, including 233 detections during the retrospective phase and 157 during the prospective phase. Following the exclusion of forty-eight prospective cases lacking parental consent, the research team analyzed detailed medical, laboratory, and therapeutic records for 342 confirmed pediatric inpatients across the participating institutions. The cohort of 342 hospitalized children exhibited a median age of 2.77 years with an interquartile range from 1.30 to 4.64 years, and male patients comprised 51.2 percent of the population. Lower respiratory tract involvement dominated clinical admissions, documented in 93.6 percent of cases, whereas upper respiratory tract diagnoses accounted for only 6.4 percent. Chronic underlying medical conditions were present in 41.5 percent of the overall cohort, though such comorbidities appeared with significantly greater frequency among children treated at the tertiary children’s hospital than in the community hospital system, recording 61.7 percent versus 19.1 percent. The specific pre-existing diagnoses included low birth weight in 15.2 percent, prematurity in 13.7 percent, asthma in 8.8 percent, congenital heart disease in 5.3 percent, chronic neurological disorders in 4.1 percent, genetic or chromosomal disorders in 1.5 percent, active malignancy in 1.2 percent, and diagnosed immunodeficiency in 0.9 percent. Clinical presentations were characterized by fever in 98.2 percent of children, lasting for an overall median duration of 4 days, alongside cough in 95.0 percent, audible wheezing in 34.2 percent, shortness of breath or dyspnea in 33.3 percent, and visible chest retractions in 20.8 percent. Laboratory evaluations demonstrated a median white blood cell count of 8.65 thousand cells per microliter and a median neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio of 1.51 across the study sites. Viral co-infections were confirmed in 43.9 percent of the children, with rhinovirus detected in 24.9 percent, parainfluenza in 9.2 percent, and adenovirus in 8.7 percent. Respiratory bacterial cultures were obtained for 179 children, yielding positive pathogenic cultures in 46.4 percent of tested individuals, predominantly Haemophilus influenzae at 14.6 percent and Moraxella catarrhalis at 14.3 percent, while Streptococcus pneumoniae was confirmed in only 4.4 percent. Radiographic abnormalities, defined as pulmonary consolidation or patchy infiltrates, were noted in 30.8 percent of evaluated chest radiographs. Hospital management entailed a median inpatient duration of 6 days, with 17.1 percent of evaluated patients requiring pediatric intensive care unit admission and staying an intensive care median of 5 days. Prescribed clinical therapies included systemic or inhaled antibiotics in 66.4 percent of children, bronchodilators in 57.9 percent, and systemic corticosteroid treatments in 17.5 percent, without any fatal outcomes recorded in the cohort. Overall, 39.8 percent of inpatients required some form of respiratory support, encompassing supplemental oxygen in 97 children and advanced respiratory support modalities in 39 cases. Advanced modalities comprised high-flow nasal cannula in 27 individuals, bilevel positive airway pressure in 7 patients, and invasive mechanical ventilation in 5 children. Multivariable regression demonstrated that the need for advanced respiratory support was independently associated with pre-existing neurological disorders, with an adjusted odds ratio of 5.76, and pulmonary consolidation or patchy infiltrations on radiographs, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.44. Epidemiological surveillance identified an annual seasonal recurrence that was remarkably consistent across all three monitored years, marked by an expansion of viral activity commencing in February, a defined peak in April, and declining detection by July. Simultaneously, analysis of patient demographics demonstrated a progressive decline in the median age of hospitalized children from 3.45 years in 2023 to 3.06 years in 2024, falling to 2.12 years by 2025. Statistical trend testing confirmed that the proportion of hospitalized infants aged zero to one year increased significantly over the three years, while the proportion of affected children older than five years dropped significantly. The authors noted that older children accounted for an elevated share of hospitalizations during the initial 2023 resurgence wave before hospital admissions reverted toward the customary younger pediatric demographic, aligning with international observations documented in Japan and other jurisdictions following post-pandemic re-emergence. Molecular sequencing and phylogenetic analysis of prospective specimens successfully characterized the fusion gene of 124 human metapneumovirus isolates, identifying genotype A in 85 specimens, representing 68.5 percent, and genotype B in 39 specimens, representing 31.5 percent. Phylogenetic trees constructed using maximum-likelihood methods on 78 complete fusion gene coding sequences demonstrated that all four global sublineages co-circulated in Taiwan, with sublineage A2.2.2 constituting the predominant lineage. Furthermore, circulating genotype B2 viruses isolated during the 2025 season were marked by two specific amino acid substitutions in the fusion protein, designated L36H and K179R, which mirrored emerging variant strains identified in regional outbreaks within mainland China during the corresponding 2024 to 2025 period. Comparative clinical analyses between genotype A and genotype B revealed broadly similar symptomatology, diagnoses, and interventions, although children with genotype B presented with a higher frequency of neurological disorders and higher median leukocyte counts. The study authors highlighted several methodological limitations that contextualize their observational conclusions, including the relatively modest number of successfully sequenced viral amplicons and the exclusive analysis of the fusion gene coding region. Because the viral attachment glycoprotein gene was not sequenced, the researchers could not verify whether the predominant A2.2.2 strains harbored the 111-nucleotide or 180-nucleotide gene duplications described in other international cohorts. Additionally, clinical specimens were unavailable for sequencing from the 2023 to 2024 period, preventing uninterrupted continuous molecular tracking across the complete three-year span. The investigators also emphasized that differences in data collection between the retrospective and prospective study phases, potential selection bias from consent requirements, single-country geographic scope, and lack of comparative pathogen controls warrant cautious interpretation of the observed age shifts, underscoring the necessity for sustained multicenter molecular surveillance to monitor ongoing viral evolution and transmission. records.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 26, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Computational Study Identifies Candidate Small Molecules Targeting Human Metapneumovirus Nucleocapsid by November 24, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Computational Study Identifies Candidate Small Molecules Targeting Human Metapneumovirus Nucleocapsid Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A computational drug discovery investigation has identified three candidate small-molecule inhibitors that demonstrate favorable binding affinity, structural stability, and drug-like properties against the nucleocapsid protein of human metapneumovirus. Human metapneumovirus, first isolated in 2001 within the family Paramyxoviridae, represents a leading cause of acute respiratory tract infections across all demographics, frequently resulting in severe bronchiolitis and pneumonia requiring hospitalization among pediatric, elderly, and immunocompromised populations. While seasonal outbreaks circulate globally and seroprevalence surveys indicate widespread infection by age five, host immunity remains incomplete, permitting lifelong reinfections transmitted via direct contact, respiratory droplets, and contaminated fomites. Despite this sustained morbidity and documented mortality risks during viral coinfection, there are currently no approved antiviral therapies or protective vaccines directed against the pathogen. Broad-spectrum antiviral treatments such as ribavirin have offered limited clinical efficacy, while monoclonal antibodies directed against the surface fusion protein encounter substantial production costs and sequence variability, accentuating the urgent requirement for targeted small-molecule therapeutics. To bypass the complications of antigenic drift observed in viral surface glycoproteins, researchers focused on the nucleocapsid protein, an indispensable structural component of human metapneumovirus. The single-stranded negative-sense RNA viral genome encodes nine proteins, including structural and nonstructural elements such as the fusion protein, attachment glycoprotein, small hydrophobic protein, matrix protein, large RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, phosphoprotein, and two nonstructural factors. The nucleocapsid protein plays a foundational role in safeguarding viral genetic material by encasing genomic RNA, preventing host immune recognition, and forming an active ribonucleoprotein replication complex alongside the viral phosphoprotein cofactor and the large polymerase enzyme. Because the nucleocapsid sequence is highly conserved across strains and serves an obligatory mechanical function in genomic encapsidation and transcriptional elongation, it represents an especially attractive antiviral target, as disruption of its binding interactions could suppress viral propagation and diminish overall clinical disease severity. The investigative team established a structured computational pipeline that integrated structure-based virtual screening, secondary redocking, continuous five-hundred-nanosecond molecular dynamics simulations, free energy calculations, and absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion predictions. Structural modeling was anchored to the high-resolution crystal structure of the monomeric, RNA-free human metapneumovirus nucleocapsid protein bound to its phosphoprotein cofactor, cataloged under Protein Data Bank identifier 5FVD at a resolution of 1.86 angstroms. Preparation of the macromolecule was executed using the DockPrep utility within UCSF Chimera, wherein crystallographic water molecules were cleared, polar hydrogens were added, protonation states of active-site residues were inspected, and energetic minimization was conducted to relieve steric clashes. Binding cavity coordinates were computed using the CASTp server, prioritizing the largest predicted pocket which incorporates functional amino acid residues such as leucine 167, tryptophan 261, isoleucine 334, and methionine 337 that participate directly in RNA association and nucleoprotein oligomerization. Virtual screening commenced across the MTiOpenScreen academic platform, evaluating fifteen hundred pre-filtered drug-like molecules from the diverse-lib library to identify chemical scaffolds with high docking affinity and adherence to Lipinski rules. The screening scores across the library spanned an energetic spectrum from minus 10.7 to positive 8.3 kilocalories per mole. From this initial assessment, the three top-ranked candidate structures were shortlisted for secondary redocking using AutoDock Vina in UCSF Chimera alongside Gamma-Fagarine, a compound selected as a comparative reference standard due to its established antiviral relevance and baseline interaction stability within the target pocket. The three candidate compounds—designated by identifiers 24,330,502, 24,292,974, and 17,515,455—exhibited primary virtual screening scores of minus 10.7, minus 10.3, and minus 10.3 kilocalories per mole, substantially surpassing the reference molecule. Secondary redocking analyses validated the docking consistency of the shortlisted molecules, yielding binding energies of minus 10.2 kilocalories per mole for compound 24,330,502, minus 10.3 kilocalories per mole for compound 24,292,974, and minus 9.6 kilocalories per mole for compound 17,515,455. In contrast, Gamma-Fagarine produced a noticeably weaker redocking score of minus 6.3 kilocalories per mole, suggesting a diminished capacity for binding site occupancy. Chemically, compound 24,330,502 corresponds to PubChem identifier 1111158, designated systematically as 3,4-dihydroisoquinolin-2(1H)-yl[5-phenyl-7-(trifluoromethyl)pyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-3-yl]methanone. Compound 24,292,974 corresponds to PubChem identifier 4292500, chemically named N-(2-(4-fluorophenyl)-4,6-dihydro-2H-thieno[3,4-c]pyrazol-3-yl)-2-oxo-2H-chromene-3-carboxamide, while compound 17,515,455 corresponds to PubChem identifier 7125864, identified as 4-benzyl-1-(4-fluorophenyl)-[1,2,4]triazolo[4,3-a]quinazolin-5(4H)-one. The reference standard Gamma-Fagarine is recorded under PubChem identifier 107936. Detailed intermolecular contact mapping carried out with the Desmond and Maestro visualization modules demonstrated intricate noncovalent interaction networks that anchored the candidate ligands within the nucleocapsid binding groove. Compound 24,330,502 established an extensive hydrophobic network involving leucine 167, isoleucine 176, valine 178, alanine 254, tryptophan 261, isoleucine 334, isoleucine 335, and methionine 337, complemented by prominent pi-pi stacking interactions with tryptophan 261. Compound 24,292,974 developed direct hydrogen bonds with threonine 170 and serine 174, while also engaging hydrophobic contacts with leucine 167, isoleucine 176, valine 178, alanine 254, tryptophan 261, isoleucine 334, and isoleucine 335, alongside dual pi-pi stacking and cation-pi interactions involving arginine 186 and tryptophan 261. Compound 17,515,455 anchored through a hydrogen bond with threonine 257, an extensive hydrophobic assembly with residues including leucine 167, alanine 254, and methionine 337, and both pi-pi stacking and cation-pi associations with arginine 186 and tryptophan 261. By comparison, Gamma-Fagarine established hydrogen bonds with serine 174, threonine 257, and arginine 260, but engaged fewer hydrophobic contacts and lacked pi-pi stacking altogether. To evaluate the conformational behavior and kinetic stability of the complexes under simulated physiological conditions, unconstrained five-hundred-nanosecond molecular dynamics simulations were conducted using Desmond and Maestro with the OPLS-2005 force field. Each solvated system was enclosed in an orthorhombic periodic boundary box of TIP3P water molecules with ten angstroms of buffer clearance, neutralized through sodium and chloride counter-ions, and adjusted to 0.15 molar sodium chloride. Systems underwent two-stage energy minimization followed by consecutive NVT equilibration at 300 Kelvin via Berendsen thermostats and NPT equilibration at one atmosphere utilizing Nosé-Hoover thermostats and Martyna-Tobias-Klein barostats. Particle mesh Ewald summations governed electrostatic forces, with van der Waals cutoffs established at ten angstroms, recording trajectories every ten picoseconds over the five-hundred-nanosecond production phase. Root mean square deviation trajectories confirmed that the top candidate complexes attained structural equilibrium across the simulation timeframe. The complex formed by compound 24,330,502 demonstrated exceptional stability, maintaining low protein and ligand root mean square deviation values below four angstroms with minimal fluctuations throughout the trajectory. Compound 24,292,974 displayed a steady protein backbone but exhibited ligand deviations that reached up to twelve angstroms, indicating dynamic conformational adjustments within the cavity. Compound 17,515,455 maintained steady coordinates before undergoing a minor deviation shift near four hundred nanoseconds consistent with localized ligand repositioning. Conversely, the Gamma-Fagarine complex exhibited profound instability, with ligand deviations surpassing thirty angstroms, reflecting weak target retention and progressive dissociation from the binding pocket. Complementary root mean square fluctuation analyses of protein residues and ligand coordinates affirmed that critical amino acids forming the binding pocket experienced minimal atomic deviation, although terminal protein segments exhibited expected flexibility. Ligand fluctuation measurements showed that compound 24,330,502 experienced the lowest internal fluctuation, confirming a rigid, well-accommodated binding posture. While compound 24,292,974 and compound 17,515,455 displayed moderate flexibility, the reference standard Gamma-Fagarine generated extreme fluctuations ranging between twelve and fifteen angstroms. Principal component analysis substantiated these dynamics across the first two eigenvectors, which accounted for substantial variance proportions. Projections for compound 24,330,502, whose first two principal components captured 54.1 percent and 15.1 percent of variance respectively, formed compact, well-defined clusters indicative of homogenous structural sampling. In contrast, Gamma-Fagarine generated widely dispersed projections spanning 56.0 percent and 18.2 percent of variance, denoting extensive structural transitions and lack of stable complexation. Thermodynamic stability was further interrogated through free energy landscape construction and structural superimposition of representative low-energy conformations against initial docked coordinates. Free energy landscape projections generated via the Geo-Measures plugin revealed that compound 24,330,502 resided within a deep, singular, concentrated energy basin, reflecting a stable state. Compounds 24,292,974 and 17,515,455 navigated multiple shallow energy minima representing permissible conformational flexibility, whereas Gamma-Fagarine yielded fragmented, shallow basins characteristic of unstable binding. Superimposition of the lowest-energy conformations extracted from simulation trajectories demonstrated minimal structural drift from original docking coordinates, yielding root mean square deviations of 1.928 angstroms for compound 24,330,502, 1.722 angstroms for compound 24,292,974, and 2.029 angstroms for compound 17,515,455, compared with 1.855 angstroms for Gamma-Fagarine. End-point binding free energy calculations performed using the Prime MM/GBSA method over the final fifty nanoseconds of trajectory confirmed robust thermodynamic affinities for the candidate molecules. Compound 17,515,455 achieved the most favorable net binding free energy of minus 74.57 plus or minus 7.81 kilocalories per mole, followed by compound 24,330,502 at minus 68.83 plus or minus 4.47 kilocalories per mole, and compound 24,292,974 at minus 45.75 plus or minus 3.61 kilocalories per mole. In stark contrast, Gamma-Fagarine yielded a significantly weaker binding free energy of minus 24.89 plus or minus 2.28 kilocalories per mole. Energetic decomposition highlighted that nonpolar forces drove complexation, with van der Waals contributions reaching minus 54.52 kilocalories per mole for compound 17,515,455 and minus 53.73 kilocalories per mole for compound 24,330,502. These were reinforced by favorable lipophilic free energies of minus 26.79 plus or minus 1.56 and minus 21.01 plus or minus 1.09 kilocalories per mole, alongside favorable electrostatic contributions for compounds 24,330,502 and 17,515,455. Pharmacokinetic and physicochemical evaluations using SwissADME revealed generally favorable drug-likeness profiles alongside specific liabilities that direct future lead optimization. All three candidate compounds demonstrated high predicted gastrointestinal absorption, absence of pan-assay interference compounds structural alerts, and identical bioavailability scores of 0.55. Compounds 24,330,502 and 24,292,974 satisfied Lipinski rule-of-five criteria with zero violations, while compound 17,515,455 exhibited a single violation. Synthetic accessibility scores ranged favorably from 2.90 to 3.57. However, the profiling flagged several optimization requirements: compounds 24,330,502 and 17,515,455 showed predicted blood-brain barrier permeability, multiple cytochrome P450 isoenzyme inhibition liabilities across CYP1A2, CYP2C19, and CYP3A4 were identified, and moderate to poor aqueous solubility classifications were recorded across thermodynamic descriptors. Crucially, the authors emphasized that these computational observations are strictly in silico predictions that cannot capture physiological complexity, requiring subsequent in vitro biophysical assays, surface plasmon resonance binding studies, cytotoxicity profiling, and cell-culture validation to confirm therapeutic efficacy against live human metapneumovirus.
